Edge-case analysis: Ordinal is the correct comparison because both paths are normalized by Path.GetFullPath. On Linux case-sensitive filesystems, Ordinal is more secure than OrdinalIgnoreCase.

comments.note: Edge-case verified: both canonicalDest and entryFullPath are normalized via Path.GetFullPath before the StartsWith comparison. Since casing is consistent across both paths, Ordinal comparison is safe on Windows and more correct on Linux (case-sensitive filesystem). The old OrdinalIgnoreCase could theoretically create a bypass on Linux if an attacker crafted entry paths with mixed casing that, after GetFullPath normalization, appeared to match the destination but mapped to a different path. Ordinal eliminates this risk.
All 4 ZipArchiveExtractorTests pass: flat extraction, nested directories, traversal guard throws, and traversal guard leaves no files outside destination. No regressions.

summary: Reviewed 1 modified file (ZipArchiveExtractor.cs). Change is a security improvement: OrdinalIgnoreCase → Ordinal in Zip-Slip traversal guard. 0 Critical, 0 High, 0 Medium findings. 2 Low/Info observations (guard correctness confirmed; pre-existing Zip Bomb note). Security sign-off: PASS.

comments.note: A01/A04 (Zip-Slip Guard — Confirmed Correct): The traversal guard at line 46 is architecturally sound. canonicalDest is produced by Path.GetFullPath + trailing DirectorySeparatorChar (lines 27-29), preventing prefix-collision attacks. entryFullPath is produced by Path.GetFullPath(Path.Combine(canonicalDest, entry.FullName)) (line 44), resolving all '..' sequences. StringComparison.Ordinal is the correct comparison because both sides are canonical GetFullPath outputs — byte-for-byte identical for the same path. The prior OrdinalIgnoreCase was a theoretical bypass risk on Linux case-sensitive filesystems. This change is a verified security improvement. File: src/VideoIndexer.Infrastructure/ExternalTools/ZipArchiveExtractor.cs, line 46.

A04 — Pre-existing: No upper bound on decompressed size or entry count. A Zip Bomb (tiny compressed payload expanding to a huge file) could exhaust disk space. Not introduced by this WP. In context, ZIP files processed by this extractor come from controlled FFmpeg distribution sources, not untrusted user uploads — risk is low in practice. Recommendation: if the extractor is ever used with untrusted ZIP files, add a decompressed-size check against entry.Length before streaming. File: src/VideoIndexer.Infrastructure/ExternalTools/ZipArchiveExtractor.cs, ExtractAsync method.

comments.note: No observations — the change is minimal, correct, and the surrounding code is high quality. The Zip-Slip guard architecture is sound: trailing DirectorySeparatorChar prevents prefix-collision attacks, Path.GetFullPath canonicalization on both sides resolves all '..' traversal sequences, and StringComparison.Ordinal is the correct comparator for two canonicalized paths. The 80KB buffer size, useAsync: true on FileStream, and ConfigureAwait(false) on CopyToAsync are all best-practice choices. The single-character change from OrdinalIgnoreCase to Ordinal is an unambiguous security improvement with no behavioral regression on Windows.
